Abstract—This paper presents two stochastic model predictive
control methods for linear time-invariant systems subject to
unbounded additive uncertainties. The new methods are developed by formulating the chance constraints into deterministic
form, which are treated in analogy with robust constraints, by
using the probabilistic reachable set. Firstly, the probabilistically
resolvable time-varying tube-based stochastic model predictive
control algorithm is designed by employing the time-varying
probabilistic reachable sets as the tubes. Secondly, by utilizing
the probabilistic positively invariant set, the probabilistically resolvable constant tube-based stochastic model predictive control
algorithm is developed by employing the constantly tightened
constraints in the entire prediction horizons. In addition, to
enhance the feasibility of the algorithms, the soft constraints
are imposed to the state initializations. The algorithm feasibility
and closed-loop stability results are provided. The efficacy of the
approaches are demonstrated by means of numerical simulations.

Abstract

We present an efficient reinforcement learning algorithm that learns the optimal admission control policy in a partially observable queueing network. Specifically, only
the arrival and departure times from the network are observable, and optimality
refers to the average holding/rejection cost in infinite horizon.
While reinforcement learning in Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes
(POMDP) is prohibitively expensive in general, we show that our algorithm has

finite-sample guarantees under sufficiently small modelapproximation error by combining linear operator learning
with convex optimization, yielding bounds that depend
on smoothness, stability, discretization error and sample
size.
Organization of the paper. Section II discusses related
work. Section III reviews the necessary background and
formalizes the continuous offline RL setting. Section IV
reviews the optimal control background and its operator
formulation underlying the O-CTRL policy update. Section V
introduces our nonparametric controlled-diffusion generator
estimator from generic state-action infinitesimal data. Section
VI combines these ingredients to derive O-CTRL. Section VII
analyzes its end-to-end learning rates. Section VIII illustrates
the theory with numerical examples. The appendix contains
the supporting proofs.

results.text:
Optimal admission control is one of the most classical control problems in queues.
It has been investigated in several works; see, e.g., [18, 19] and the references therein.
However, these works consider the case where the model parameters are known, i.e.,
no learning mechanism is used. The novelty of our approach is to leverage i) Norton’s
equivalence theorem for closed product-form queueing networks [20] and ii) the efficiency
of reinforcement learning in MDPs with the structure of birth-and-death processes
[17]. More specifically, our result is achieved by using Norton’s theorem to replace the
whole network by a single load-dependent queue in its stationary regime and relies on
the mixing time τmix of the network to apply this equivalence every τmix time-steps.
The key observation is that Norton’s theorem helps us to somewhat cast the original
partially-observable MDP to a standard (fully-observable) MDP. In other words, the
resulting asymptotically equivalent POMDP becomes an MDP with the structure of a
birth and death process.

results.text:
Optimal admission control is one of the most classical control problems in queues.
It has been investigated in several works; see, e.g., [18, 19] and the references therein.
However, these works consider the case where the model parameters are known, i.e.,
no learning mechanism is used. The novelty of our approach is to leverage i) Norton’s
equivalence theorem for closed product-form queueing networks [20] and ii) the efficiency
of reinforcement learning in MDPs with the structure of birth-and-death processes
[17]. More specifically, our result is achieved by using Norton’s theorem to replace the
whole network by a single load-dependent queue in its stationary regime and relies on
the mixing time τmix of the network to apply this equivalence every τmix time-steps.
The key observation is that Norton’s theorem helps us to somewhat cast the original
partially-observable MDP to a standard (fully-observable) MDP. In other words, the
resulting asymptotically equivalent POMDP becomes an MDP with the structure of a
birth and death process.

IV. THE OPTIMAL CONTROL PERSPECTIVE
This section reviews established stochastic optimal control
concepts in the operator-theoretic form used by O-CTRL. Although fixed-policy evaluation is linear in the reward through
Eq. (9), policy optimization in RL is generally nonlinear
and challenging because the policy-to-value map π 7→V is
nonlinear. In contrast, under control-affine dynamics and a
strongly convex action penalty, the Hamiltonian maximization
over a convex admissible action set admits a unique global
maximizer characterized by the Fenchel conjugate. When
this conjugate is explicitly available, it yields a closed-form
policy update offering simplicity and tractability analogous
to LQR. Moreover, because continuous-time Q-functions are
ill-defined as the discretization vanishes [50], our operatortheoretic HJB formulation avoids dependence on an arbitrary
time increment or surrogate Q-function [9], [50], [7].

offline RL includes both model-based [4], [5] and modelfree methods [6]. Available continuous-time methods are
mostly model-free [7] or lack a learning theory. For a

explicitly connect continuous-time RL with stochastic optimal
control, however, either focus on linear-quadratic settings [10]
or require online interaction with the environment [11].
Numerical schemes for optimal control also typically lack
a statistical learning theory relating value-function error to
problem regularity and sample complexity [12], [13], [14].
This leaves the nonlinear offline setting without comparable
end-to-end guarantees. Direct numerical solution of HJB
equations is also limited by the curse of dimensionality, since
grid-based state discretizations grow exponentially with the
state dimension.

on problem properties and sample size. In discrete time,
offline RL includes both model-based [4], [5] and modelfree methods [6]. Available continuous-time methods are
mostly model-free [7] or lack a learning theory. For a
comprehensive review of offline RL, we refer to [3]. Under
standard technical assumptions, RL can be viewed through the
lens of optimal control, with the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman
(HJB) equation providing a central link to the numerical
analysis of optimal control [8], [9]. Existing results that
explicitly connect continuous-time RL with stochastic optimal
control, however, either focus on linear-quadratic settings [10]
or require online interaction with the environment [11].
Numerical schemes for optimal control also typically lack
a statistical learning theory relating value-function error to
problem regularity and sample complexity [12], [13], [14].
This leaves the nonlinear offline setting without comparable
end-to-end guarantees. Direct numerical solution of HJB
equations is also limited by the curse of dimensionality, since
grid-based state discretizations grow exponentially with the
state dimension.

In discrete-time RL, related
operator constructions support conditional mean embedding
Bellman updates and policy mirror descent [33], [23], but
remain tied to discrete-time Bellman operators or finite action
sets [23]. The closest continuous-time predecessor is the
kernel infinitesimal-generator framework of [34]. That work
connects generator learning to control, but under a restrictive
data-collection protocol separating autonomous and control
directions and without an end-to-end perturbation bound for
the resulting value function. Here, the controlled generator
is learned from generic offline tuples involving state, action,
and infinitesimal state change..

IV. THE OPTIMAL CONTROL PERSPECTIVE
This section reviews established stochastic optimal control
concepts in the operator-theoretic form used by O-CTRL. Although fixed-policy evaluation is linear in the reward through
Eq. (9), policy optimization in RL is generally nonlinear
and challenging because the policy-to-value map π 7→V is
nonlinear. In contrast, under control-affine dynamics and a
strongly convex action penalty, the Hamiltonian maximization
over a convex admissible action set admits a unique global
maximizer characterized by the Fenchel conjugate. When
this conjugate is explicitly available, it yields a closed-form
policy update offering simplicity and tractability analogous
to LQR. Moreover, because continuous-time Q-functions are
ill-defined as the discretization vanishes [50], our operatortheoretic HJB formulation avoids dependence on an arbitrary
time increment or surrogate Q-function [9], [50], [7].
